Biological validation is appropriate but somewhat generic relative to the sophistication of the materials hypothesis. Minor score deductions reflect these mechanistic ambiguities rather than feasibility concerns.

Hypothesis:
We hypothesize that **operationally defined limited pepsin proteolysis**—implemented as a tunable “proteolysis window” (pH, temperature, enzyme:substrate ratio, and time) and **verified by direct cleavage-site mapping**—will preferentially reduce **telopeptide-derived heterogeneity** in collagen preparations while preserving the **triple-helical Gly–X–Y core**, thereby producing pepsin-soluble collagen (PSC) with (i) **narrower molecular weight/polydispersity profiles**, and (ii) **more cooperative helix–coil unfolding** (sharper DSC/CD transitions) relative to acid-solubilized collagen (ASC) and conventional PSC.

Mechanistic rationale: Collagen telopeptides are structurally flexible, variably crosslinked, and enriched in species- and tissue-dependent post-translational modifications, making them major contributors to extraction-to-extraction heterogeneity and broadened thermal transitions. Under mildly acidic conditions where the triple helix remains kinetically protected, pepsin-accessible cleavage is expected to occur predominantly in **non-helical, solvent-exposed regions** (operational target: N/C telopeptides), decreasing heterogeneous intermolecular associations/aggregation and yielding a more uniform population of triple helices. Importantly, the proposal does **not** assume enzyme “site-specificity”; instead, it defines success as meeting **pre-registered acceptance criteria**: (a) measurable enrichment of telopeptide-derived peptides in the pepsin-released fraction and depletion in the retained collagen fraction, and (b) no detectable cleavage within predefined helical-core marker peptides by LC–MS mapping. If these criteria are met, improvements in homogeneity and thermal cooperativity can be causally attributed to limited proteolysis rather than to hydroxyproline content differences, batch variation, or helix damage.
Plan:
Step 1 — Source selection, batch structure, and parallel extraction arms (ASC vs PSC vs limited-proteolysis PSC).
1.1. Source: collagen-rich marine by-products from a single species and tissue type per experimental block (e.g., tropical fish skin) to minimize compositional confounding; ≥3 biological batches (different lots/days) to model batch effects.
1.2. Parallel arms:
  A) ASC: standard acid extraction (acetic acid; temperature controlled at 4–10 °C).
  B) Conventional PSC: literature-like pepsin extraction condition (benchmark).
  C) Limited-proteolysis PSC (LP-PSC): a designed “proteolysis window” screen varying:
     • pH: 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 (acidic range relevant to pepsin activity and helix stability)
     • Temperature: 4 °C vs 10 °C (to reduce helix destabilization)
     • Pepsin:collagen (w/w): 0.1%, 0.5%, 1.0%
     • Time: 0.5 h, 2 h, 6 h
  Design: fractional factorial or response-surface design (pre-registered) to identify conditions meeting acceptance criteria (Step 2).
1.3. Concentration normalization: hydroxyproline assay for collagen mass normalization across arms (used for dosing and CD/DSC loading), while explicitly treating hydroxyproline as a covariate (not as a mechanistic proxy).

Step 2 — Direct verification module for “limited proteolysis” (mandatory causality anchor).
2.1. SDS-PAGE acceptance check (rapid screen): reducing SDS-PAGE of extracted collagen fractions to confirm preservation of α1/α2 chain pattern consistent with type I collagen and absence of extensive low-MW smearing indicative of over-digestion.
2.2. LC–MS peptide mapping to localize cleavage (primary verification):
  • Sample sets: (i) soluble released peptide fraction after pepsin step, (ii) purified collagen fraction post-salt precipitation/dialysis.
  • Workflow: enzymatic digestion for mapping (e.g., trypsin) followed by LC–MS/MS; search against species-appropriate collagen I sequences (or de novo-assisted mapping if incomplete annotation).
  • Operational definitions:
     – “Telopeptide peptides”: peptides mapping to annotated/known N- and C-terminal non-helical regions and adjacent crosslink-prone segments.
     – “Helical-core marker peptides”: a pre-specified panel of peptides mapping to central Gly–X–Y repeat regions distant from termini.
  • Acceptance criteria (pre-registered):
     (a) ≥X% (e.g., ≥30–50% threshold to be finalized after pilot) reduction of telopeptide peptide spectral counts/intensity in the retained collagen fraction vs ASC/conventional PSC, AND
     (b) no statistically significant increase (vs ASC) in cleavage signatures within helical-core marker peptides (e.g., no new semi-tryptic/non-tryptic termini within core markers above defined false-discovery thresholds).
  • Optional orthogonal confirmation (if available): telopeptide-specific immunoassay/ELISA for N- and C-telopeptides or targeted MRM for selected telopeptide peptides.
2.3. Decision gate: only conditions that pass acceptance criteria proceed to full structural/biophysical characterization; failing conditions are classified as “over-digested” or “under-processed” and used to validate dose–response relationships.

Step 3 — Time-course sampling strategy replacing “in situ CD” (turbidity-controlled CD/DSC pipeline).
3.1. Time-course collection: for each LP-PSC condition, collect aliquots at defined times (e.g., 0, 0.5, 2, 6 h).
3.2. Clarification SOP prior to CD/FTIR:
  • Centrifugation: e.g., 10,000–20,000 g, 10–20 min, 4 °C.
  • Filtration: 0.22–0.45 µm low-protein-binding filter (material specified in protocol).
  • Turbidity/absorbance thresholds: measure UV–Vis absorbance; proceed to CD only if A320 (or equivalent scattering proxy) is below a pre-set threshold; otherwise repeat clarification or dilute to threshold.
  • Fixed CD parameters: constant pathlength (e.g., 0.1–1 mm depending on concentration), constant ionic strength/pH buffer for measurement (post-clarification buffer exchange if needed), and matched baselines.
3.3. CD readouts (secondary structural readout):
  • Far-UV CD scan to confirm triple helix signature (e.g., positive band near ~220 nm).
  • Temperature-ramp CD (post-clarification) to estimate unfolding profile and cooperativity (e.g., normalized ellipticity vs temperature; fit to sigmoidal/van’t Hoff-type models), explicitly correcting for baseline drift using buffer-only and heat-treated denatured controls.

Step 4 — Thermal stability and structural integrity (DSC primary; CD secondary; optional FTIR).
4.1. DSC (primary Tm/Td):
  • Standardized collagen concentration (hydroxyproline-normalized), buffer conditions matched across samples.
  • Outputs: Tm/Td, transition enthalpy (ΔH), and transition width (cooperativity proxy).
4.2. FTIR (optional orthogonal): amide I/III and triple-helix-associated band ratios to confirm preservation of secondary structure across ASC vs PSC vs LP-PSC.

Step 5 — SEC/GPC specification and aggregation controls (explicit native vs denatured objective).
5.1. Define objective and matched method:
  • Primary objective: quantify **molecular weight distribution/polydispersity** relevant to solution-processability and scaffold fabrication.
  • Two complementary SEC modes:
     A) Denaturing SEC (robust chain distribution): separates α-chains and higher aggregates under denaturing conditions to avoid column interaction artifacts.
     B) “Native-like” SEC (conditional): attempts to preserve higher-order assemblies/triple helices; treated as exploratory and only interpreted if aggregation/interaction controls pass.
5.2. Denaturing SEC (recommended as primary PDI metric):
  • Mobile phase: e.g., 4–6 M guanidine-HCl or urea-based system with defined ionic strength; temperature controlled.
  • Column: SEC media compatible with denaturants (explicit column chemistry/pore range selected for 100–1000 kDa regime; finalize based on instrument availability).
  • Calibration: protein standards and/or collagen standards; report apparent MW and PDI.
5.3. Native-like SEC (exploratory, with stringent controls):
  • Column: inert/hydrophilic SEC column designed to reduce protein adsorption.
  • Mobile phase: mild acid/salt composition (defined pH and ionic strength) plus additive strategy if needed to minimize non-specific interactions.
  • Temperature: maintained below denaturation threshold.
  • Aggregation checks: inline MALS (if available) or fraction collection followed by DLS to quantify hydrodynamic size; define exclusion criteria if large aggregates dominate.
5.4. Injection controls: standardized injection concentration range to avoid concentration-dependent aggregation; replicate injections to quantify run-to-run variability.

Step 6 — Pre-registered statistical modeling to separate cleavage effects from composition/batch effects.
6.1. Model structure: mixed-effects models with batch as random effect; fixed effects include (i) cleavage extent metrics (telopeptide removal index from LC–MS), (ii) hydroxyproline content, (iii) extraction arm/condition, and (iv) interaction terms where justified.
6.2. Primary endpoints:
  • DSC: Tm/Td and transition width (cooperativity).
  • SEC: PDI (primary from denaturing SEC; secondary from native-like SEC if valid).
6.3. Mediation/causality logic (within observational constraints): test whether cleavage extent mediates the relationship between extraction condition and (Tm width, PDI), while controlling for hydroxyproline and batch.

Step 7 — Deliverable decision criteria.
7.1. LP-PSC is deemed superior to ASC/conventional PSC only if:
  • Cleavage acceptance criteria are met (Step 2), AND
  • DSC shows significantly sharper transition (reduced width) and/or increased Tm (species-dependent) without loss of ΔH consistent with helix preservation, AND
  • SEC shows reduced PDI relative to ASC and conventional PSC.
7.2. If DSC indicates reduced stability or LC–MS indicates core cleavage, conditions are classified as helix-damaging and excluded from “optimized LP-PSC.”
Feasibility:
1) Mechanistic and empirical grounding: Prior marine collagen studies consistently show that PSC often exhibits higher yield and altered composition relative to ASC, and that thermal stability correlates with imino acids/hydroxyproline and structural integrity. However, reviewer concerns about over-attributing effects to “site-specific” cleavage are addressed by reframing the mechanism around an **operationally testable limited-proteolysis window** and by making **LC–MS mapping + SDS-PAGE** a mandatory decision gate.

2) Addressing pepsin broad specificity: The proposal explicitly anticipates context-dependent susceptibility (pH/temperature/helix stability) and therefore uses a designed parameter screen plus **acceptance criteria** (telopeptide depletion with no helical-core cleavage signal) rather than assuming specificity. This makes the key claim falsifiable and prevents inferential leaps.

3) CD practicality in complex matrices: The “in situ” claim is replaced with a **time-resolved, clarified-aliquot workflow** with explicit centrifugation/filtration and turbidity thresholds, fixed pathlength, and baseline/scattering controls—aligning CD readouts with optical constraints of crude extraction liquors.

4) SEC/GPC realism and interpretability: Because collagen–column interactions and aggregation can invalidate ‘native’ SEC, the plan specifies a **primary denaturing SEC mode** for reliable PDI/chain distribution and an explicitly labeled **exploratory native-like SEC** only if aggregation/interaction controls (MALS/DLS, temperature control, injection limits) pass. This directly addresses reviewer concerns about nontrivial “helix-preserving” SEC.

5) Orthogonal structure–function validation: DSC is designated as the **primary thermal stability metric**, CD as secondary for helix signature/cooperativity, and optional FTIR as an orthogonal confirmation. This triangulation reduces reliance on any single method.

6) Separation of confounds (hydroxyproline, crosslink remnants, batch/species variation): Hydroxyproline is used for concentration normalization but is also modeled as a covariate; batch is treated as a random effect; and cleavage extent is explicitly quantified and incorporated into pre-registered models. This design enables distinguishing whether thermal/cooperativity changes track with **telopeptide removal** versus compositional or damage-related artifacts.

Collectively, these revisions convert the central premise into a rigorous, falsifiable workflow where improved homogeneity and thermal behavior can be causally linked to verified limited proteolysis rather than assumed enzymatic selectivity or uncontrolled measurement artifacts.
Critique: Methodologically, the proposal is strong: it converts a historically hand-wavy PSC/ASC comparison into a falsifiable limited-proteolysis optimization with explicit decision gates (SDS-PAGE + LC–MS mapping) and appropriate orthogonal biophysics (DSC primary, CD secondary). The factorial/response-surface framing is appropriate for pepsin’s broad specificity. However, several elements remain under-specified in ways that can materially affect interpretability and feasibility: (i) the LC–MS acceptance criteria rely on spectral counts/intensity shifts that may be dominated by digestion/mapping biases, sequence incompleteness in marine collagen, and PTM/crosslink-derived search failures; without a quantitative, peptide-level normalization strategy and explicit control for pepsin carryover/autoproteolysis, the “telopeptide removal index” risks being noisy or systematically biased. (ii) The claim that reduced PDI and sharper DSC transitions will be attributable to telopeptide depletion is plausible, but alternative mechanisms (selective loss of damaged/oxidized molecules, removal of non-collagenous proteins/proteoglycans, changes in ionic environment after processing, differential aggregation state) are not fully ruled out with dedicated controls. (iii) The SEC plan is directionally correct (denaturing primary), but still lacks concrete column/pore-range selection criteria, recovery/adsorption controls, and a defined PDI calculation approach for collagen (which often violates assumptions behind simple polymer PDI metrics). (iv) Statistical mediation language is ambitious given small batch counts (≥3 lots) and high-dimensional condition screens; power and multiplicity control are not addressed, risking overinterpretation of condition effects. Overall, the logic chain is coherent and the engineering is above-standard, but quantitation/controls around LC–MS mapping and the analysis plan need tightening to secure causal attribution.

Hypothesis: Cholestasis-associated bile acid accumulation primes cholangiocytes and liver-resident macrophages for exaggerated TWEAK/FN14-dependent chemokine output, but leukocyte recruitment is ultimately controlled by the *bioavailable* (free) fraction and spatial gradient structure of a small set of receptor-convergent chemoattractants (CCR1/CCR5, CCR2, CXCR2 axes) concentrated in the periportal/bile-duct niche. We hypothesize that (i) TWEAK/FN14 signaling contributes a quantifiable, mechanistically attributable portion of the periportal chemoattractant drive; and (ii) within that program, CCL3 (MIP-1α) is a *sufficient* recruitment determinant only in disease states where CCR1/CCR5 signaling is not fully compensated by CCR2/CXCR2 ligands. Therefore, a protease-activatable, ECM-tethered chemokine sink is expected to be effective only if it (a) achieves a threshold fractional depletion of *free* CCL3 (not total CCL3) in periportal interstitial fluid and (b) is activated by a cholestasis-enriched cleavage event that is ≥10–20× more probable in cholestatic periportal ECM than in nonhepatic inflammatory milieus. Mechanistically, the refined approach overcomes redundancy and off-target activation risk by (1) establishing a receptor-axis attribution/epistasis map (CCR1/CCR5 vs CCR2 vs CXCR2) to define whether CCL3 depletion can meaningfully reduce infiltrates beyond compensation, (2) using in situ degradomics to identify a cholestasis-enriched cleavage sequence rather than assuming canonical MMP/ADAM motifs, and (3) enforcing periportal confinement via quantitatively modeled matrix-binding pharmacokinetics (local molarity and residence time matched to CCL3 production/clearance), so that even if systemic proteases exist, activation and effective binding are spatially constrained to the bile-duct injury niche.
Plan:
PHASE 0 (Hard go/no-go de-risking before full 6P4-Sink build)

0.1 Define whether TWEAK/FN14 materially contributes to the cholestatic chemokine program (BDL and DDC; receptor-axis attribution).
- Models: (i) BDL (acute, strong periportal inflammation), (ii) DDC diet (ductular reaction, chronic injury) with matched timepoints capturing early recruitment and later fibrosis (e.g., BDL day 3/7/14; DDC week 1/3/6).
- FN14 perturbation: (a) anti-FN14 blocking antibody dosing to cover the recruitment window (pharmacokinetics verified by serum trough levels), and/or (b) Fn14-/- (or conditional Fn14 deletion in cholangiocytes and myeloid lineages if available).
- Readouts:
  (1) Unbiased chemokine profiling in liver tissue homogenate + liver interstitial fluid (microdialysis) + plasma using multiplex Luminex/Olink plus targeted LC–MS/MS quantification for key ligands: CCL3, CCL4, CCL5 (CCR1/CCR5); CCL2/7 (CCR2); CXCL1/2 (CXCR2).
  (2) Single-cell RNA-seq (or targeted scRNA panel) + spatial transcriptomics (periportal vs parenchymal segmentation) to identify the dominant ligand-producing compartments and whether they are FN14-dependent.
  (3) Receptor-pathway attribution: flow cytometry of infiltrates for CCR1/CCR5/CCR2/CXCR2 expression, and ligand–receptor inference integrating scRNA + spatial data.
- Go/no-go gate A (FN14 dependence): proceed only if FN14 perturbation reduces (i) periportal chemokine output and (ii) infiltrate burden by a pre-specified margin in at least one model (e.g., ≥25–30% reduction in Ly6C+ monocytes and/or neutrophils at peak recruitment), establishing that the upstream node is relevant and that downstream chemokines are meaningfully engaged.

0.2 Test *chemokine sufficiency* of CCL3 depletion versus compensation by CCR2/CXCR2 ligands (epistasis/neutralization framework).
- Experimental design (BDL and DDC; powered for infiltrate endpoints):
  Arms include: (i) isotype control, (ii) anti-CCL3 neutralization (or Ccl3-/- if feasible), (iii) anti-CCL2 or CCR2 inhibitor, (iv) anti-CXCL1/2 or CXCR2 inhibitor, (v) combined anti-CCL3 + CCR2 block, (vi) combined anti-CCL3 + CXCR2 block.
- Endpoints:
  (1) Infiltrate quantification: flow cytometry (Ly6C+ monocytes, neutrophils, macrophage subsets), immunohistology with spatial mapping (periportal density gradients).
  (2) Chemotaxis functional endpoint: ex vivo transwell migration of primary monocytes/neutrophils toward liver interstitial fluid (from each arm) with and without CCR1/CCR5 antagonists to isolate CCR1/CCR5-dependent chemotaxis.
  (3) Bioavailable ligand measurement: quantify *free* CCL3 (and free CCL2/CXCL1) in interstitial fluid by equilibrium binding/competition assay (e.g., capture of free ligand with excess immobilized receptor ectodomain or high-affinity antibody under conditions that do not dissociate complexes), and total ligand by denaturing ELISA.
- Quantitative sufficiency threshold (Go/no-go gate B): define and validate the required fractional reduction of *free* CCL3 to produce a measurable drop in infiltrates. Proceed only if:
  (i) CCL3 depletion alone yields ≥20% reduction in periportal infiltrate burden OR
  (ii) CCL3 depletion shows clear epistasis indicating it is a necessary component (e.g., adding CCL3 depletion to CCR2/CXCR2 blockade provides a statistically significant additional reduction), and
  (iii) a dose–response relationship ties infiltrate reduction to a target free-CCL3 depletion threshold (e.g., ≥60–80% decrease in free CCL3 in interstitial fluid at peak recruitment).
- Decision output: if redundancy makes CCL3 insufficient, pivot while preserving the platform concept by retargeting the binding core to a CCR1/CCR5 ligand set (e.g., dual CCL3/CCL5) or to the empirically dominant axis (CCR2 or CXCR2), but only after completing Phase 0 mapping.

0.3 Identify a cholestasis-enriched cleavage event with ≥10–20× activation ratio (degradomics-driven, periportal ECM-resolved).
- Sample acquisition: periportal/bile-duct region microdissection (laser capture microdissection) from BDL and DDC livers, plus controls: healthy liver, and nonhepatic inflamed tissues where systemic off-target activation is plausible (e.g., inflamed colon in DSS colitis, inflamed lung in LPS/bleomycin model, inflamed skin wound).
- N-terminomics/degradomics pipeline:
  (1) Enrich and map neo-N-termini using TMT-based N-terminomics (e.g., TAILS or HUNTER approach) on ECM-enriched fractions.
  (2) Infer dominant cleavage motifs and candidate protease classes; cross-validate with activity-based probes (MMP/ADAM/cathepsin serine protease panels) and inhibitor sensitivity in ex vivo tissue slices.
  (3) Select 2–3 candidate cleavage sequences that are (a) enriched in cholestatic periportal ECM and (b) low in nonhepatic inflamed tissues.
- Go/no-go gate C (specificity): choose a single lead cleavage sequence only if ex vivo cleavage kinetics (kcat/Km proxy using FRET-quenched peptide substrates) show ≥10–20× higher cleavage rate in cholestatic periportal ECM/tissue slices than in each off-target inflamed tissue, and if cleavage is suppressible by a defined inhibitor profile consistent with the inferred protease class.

PHASE 1 (Minimal viable sink prototypes and quantitative localization—before full protein optimization)

1.1 Build “proto-sinks” to validate activation + confinement without committing to full directed evolution.
- Construct architecture (recombinant protein):
  (A) Chemokine-binding: start with wild-type 6P4 (or best-available baseline) fused to an Fc-silent scaffold (e.g., IgG4-Fc with effector silencing) to extend half-life locally while minimizing FcγR activation.
  (B) Protease gate: N-terminal autoinhibitory mask (15–30 aa) positioned to sterically occlude the predicted binding interface; connect via the *degradomics-derived* lead cleavage sequence (from Phase 0.3). Include a non-cleavable scrambled-site control.
  (C) Matrix tether: incorporate a defined ECM-binding module with tunable affinity (e.g., collagen-binding domain with KD in the low nM–µM range). Produce 2–3 tether variants spanning affinities to empirically tune retention vs penetration.

1.2 Quantitative pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) localization model for periportal interstitial molarity.
- Define required local sink concentration from measured endogenous CCL3 kinetics:
  Inputs measured in Phase 0: interstitial fluid CCL3 concentration range (peak and baseline), production/clearance estimates (time-course microdialysis), and diffusion constraints in periportal ECM.
- Model objective: achieve free-CCL3 depletion threshold (from Go/no-go gate B) with a safety margin while limiting systemic exposure.
- Experimental validation:
  (i) Inject fluorescently labeled proto-sink (cleavable vs non-cleavable) via a delivery route selected for periportal exposure (see 1.3) and quantify liver retention, periportal enrichment, and plasma leakage (whole-organ IVIS + quantitative fluorescence in homogenates + confocal on tissue sections).
  (ii) Determine effective residence time (t1/2 in liver ECM) and penetration depth from portal tracts into parenchyma.
- Go/no-go gate D (localization): proceed only if periportal retention yields interstitial concentrations predicted to exceed the required sink molarity for ≥24–72 h (aligned to recruitment kinetics), while systemic levels remain below a pre-set fraction (e.g., <10% of liver interstitial concentration).

1.3 Replace vague delivery with an explicit, tested localization strategy.
- Primary strategy (matrix-first, not cell-entry-first): local ECM-depot delivery tuned by matrix-binding rather than bile-duct cell targeting.
  Option A: peribiliary/periportal injectable shear-thinning hydrogel depot (hyaluronan-based or peptide hydrogel) loaded with proto-sink; release controlled by mesh size and sink tether affinity.
  Option B: intravenous dosing relying on strong ECM affinity plus size-exclusion to bias retention in injured periportal matrix; only acceptable if gate D localization criteria are met.
- Rationale: GalNAc-hepatocyte targeting is explicitly avoided because the therapeutic compartment is periportal ECM; the program requires extracellular localization, not hepatocyte internalization.

PHASE 2 (Full 6P4-Sink engineering—only if Phase 0–1 gates pass)

2.1 Directed evolution to achieve the binding potency implied by the required free-CCL3 depletion.
- Library design: focused saturation mutagenesis on solvent-exposed loops predicted (AlphaFold2 + interface prediction) to contact CCL3; maintain scaffold stability (thermal shift assays; expression yield threshold).
- Display/selection:
  (i) Yeast surface display with decreasing CCL3 concentrations to drive KD into the low nM range, with kinetic selection for slow koff (to sustain sequestration under flow).
  (ii) Counter-selection against CCL4/CCL5 to control off-target CCR1/CCR5 ligand depletion *unless* Phase 0 indicates multi-ligand capture is required to overcome redundancy; in that case, deliberately evolve a defined multi-specific profile aligned to the sufficiency map.
- Functional potency metric (not just KD): ability to reduce CCR1/CCR5 reporter activation in a cell-based assay using cholestatic interstitial fluid as input.

2.2 Protease-gate integration and specificity validation.
- Insert the single degradomics-derived cleavage sequence into the mask linker; include a secondary “AND-gate” variant if needed (two-step unmasking requiring two independent cleavage events) if off-target activation remains a concern.
- Validate activation:
  (i) Ex vivo cleavage in cholestatic periportal tissue slices vs off-target inflamed tissues (quantitative mass spec of cleavage products + FRET reporter readout).
  (ii) In vivo activation imaging using a quenched fluorescent reporter built into the mask region; quantify activation spatially (periportal vs systemic organs).
- Go/no-go gate E (in vivo specificity): require ≥10× higher activation signal (normalized to dose) in cholestatic liver vs each off-target inflamed tissue tested.

2.3 ECM anchoring optimization.
- Tune matrix-binding affinity to maximize periportal retention without preventing penetration into the relevant ECM microdomain.
- Empirical mapping: intravital microscopy (where feasible) or high-resolution ex vivo imaging to quantify distribution relative to FN14+ cells and CCL3-producing compartments identified in Phase 0.

PHASE 3 (Mechanism, efficacy, and safety benchmarking with redundancy-aware comparators)

3.1 Mechanism-of-action confirmation: gradient collapse and free-ligand depletion.
- Microphysiological system: human bile-acid–stressed cholangiocyte + macrophage co-culture with controlled TWEAK stimulation; integrate microfluidic gradient chamber.
- Readouts:
  (i) Quantify free vs total CCL3 in the microenvironment.
  (ii) Live leukocyte chemotaxis assays with CCR1/CCR5 blockade to confirm that observed migration changes map to the intended axis.
  (iii) Verify that upstream cytokine production is not broadly suppressed (profile TNF, IL-1β, IL-6), consistent with a sink mechanism rather than global immunosuppression.

3.2 In vivo efficacy in BDL and DDC aligned to the sufficiency map.
- Primary endpoints: periportal infiltrate burden (flow + spatial histology), liver injury (ALT/AST, bilirubin, bile acids), and fibrosis progression (Sirius Red, hydroxyproline, α-SMA) across the recruitment-to-fibrosis timeline.
- Comparator arms:
  (i) systemic anti-TWEAK or anti-FN14,
  (ii) non-cleavable masked sink control,
  (iii) if Phase 0 reveals redundancy, include an axis-appropriate comparator (CCR2 or CXCR2 inhibition) to contextualize effect size and interpret compensation.

3.3 Safety and regeneration preservation.
- Regeneration/wound healing: hepatocyte proliferation (Ki67), ductular reaction (KRT19/SOX9), and bile-duct repair indices.
- Immune competence: ex vivo LPS challenge of splenocytes/whole blood to ensure no systemic immunoparesis.
- Off-target activation surveillance: quantify activated sink signal and free-chemokine perturbation in off-target organs, especially in parallel nonhepatic inflammation models used in Phase 0.3.

PIVOT RULES (pre-specified)
- If Go/no-go B fails (CCL3 not sufficient): retarget binding to empirically dominant ligand(s) or build a multi-ligand sink matched to the receptor-axis sufficiency map while keeping the same protease-gate + ECM-tether architecture.
- If Go/no-go C/E fails (activation not cholestasis-enriched): implement an AND-gate (dual cleavage) or abandon protease gating in favor of purely matrix-restricted depot dosing with non-activatable but tightly localized sink, only if systemic leakage remains below threshold in Gate D.
- If Gate D fails (cannot reach/maintain local molarity): prioritize hydrogel depot + higher-affinity ECM tether and/or increased dosing frequency; if still insufficient, terminate rather than proceed to expensive directed evolution.
Feasibility: This revision converts the proposal’s key assumptions into measurable constraints with pre-specified stopping rules. (1) Chemokine sufficiency is no longer presumed: FN14 perturbation plus unbiased chemokine profiling, receptor-axis attribution (CCR1/CCR5/CCR2/CXCR2), and neutralization/KO epistasis in *both* BDL and DDC establish whether CCL3 depletion can reduce recruitment beyond compensation and quantifies the required fractional reduction in *free* CCL3. This directly addresses redundancy concerns and prevents overinvestment if the biology does not support a single-ligand sink. (2) Protease-gating specificity is de-risked by degradomics (N-terminomics) on periportal ECM to identify cholestasis-enriched cleavage events rather than relying on generic MMP/ADAM/cathepsin motifs; the ≥10–20× activation ratio requirement against nonhepatic inflamed tissues operationalizes the reviewer’s specificity standard. (3) Delivery/localization is grounded in a matrix-binding PK/PD model and experimentally measured periportal retention/penetration, replacing vague ‘bile-duct targeted LNPs’ with a compartment-appropriate strategy (ECM depot and tunable ECM affinity) and explicitly defining required local molarity and residence time relative to endogenous CCL3 kinetics. Only after these gates are satisfied does the plan proceed to full directed evolution and in vivo efficacy, ensuring that engineering effort is aligned to validated biological sufficiency and activation specificity.
Critique: This is a strong, de-risked engineering/biology co-design with explicit go/no-go gates that directly address redundancy, spatial biology, and off-target activation—common failure modes for chemokine-targeting biologics. The main deductions are: (1) the central measurand “free CCL3” in liver interstitial fluid is technically under-specified and potentially confounded (rapid rebinding, glycosaminoglycan/ECM sequestration, heteromerization with other chemokines, and sampling artifacts from microdialysis recovery), risking ambiguous PK/PD linkage; (2) the ≥10–20× cleavage-enrichment requirement is appropriate but may be difficult to realize across heterogeneous cholestatic lesions and across multiple nonhepatic inflammatory controls—there is a real risk the identified motif reports tissue accessibility/ECM remodeling rather than disease-specific protease biology; (3) the plan assumes CCR1/CCR5 axis convergence onto a small ligand set, but does not fully address additional attractant systems prominent in cholestasis (e.g., CX3CL1/CX3CR1, S1P, complement fragments, LTB4) that could dominate recruitment even when CCR1/CCR5/CCR2/CXCR2 are mapped, potentially causing false-negative interpretation of sink efficacy; (4) proto-sink architecture choices (Fc-silent, tether affinities, masking length) are plausible but lack quantitative starting specifications (target KD range, on/off rates under flow, target ECM KD range tied to diffusion/penetration constraints, acceptable liver:plasma exposure ratio by dose), which makes the engineering path less tightly constrained than the biological gating suggests.

Hypothesis:
Engineering a Diels–Alderase for acrylate dienophiles with high enantioselectivity will be enabled by a binding-coupled, genetically encoded intramolecular active-site “staple” that quantitatively narrows the enzyme’s conformational ensemble into a single, chiral near-attack-conformation (NAC) cage. To directly address turnover coupling, we will implement and compare two explicitly defined operational modes:

(Mode 1: Reversible, steady-state gated stapling) A reversible covalent tether (dynamic staple) that forms predominantly in the acrylate-bound closed state and dissociates on the catalytic timescale after product release. This ensures that the enzyme cycles through open (substrate entry/product exit) → closed+stapled (NAC enrichment/TS stabilization) → open (release/reset), preserving true binding-gated operation under steady-state.

(Mode 2: Substrate-triggered maturation/locking) An effectively irreversible crosslink (e.g., IEDDA or thioether) that converts an initially dynamic scaffold into a permanently “matured” chiral pocket after a priming exposure to acrylate. Here the central claim is reframed as substrate-triggered conformational maturation that yields a stable high-ee catalytic state. This mode is tested explicitly by comparing pre-stapled vs post-stapled kinetics/ee and by determining whether ee correlates with crosslink fraction and not merely with generic rigidification.

Mechanistically, in both modes acrylate engagement must (i) template short-range reactive proximity between two engineered anchor residues flanking the dienophile pocket, (ii) lock the relative orientation of mobile pocket elements (loop/helix gate) that otherwise permit multiple acrylate poses, and (iii) enforce a single facial presentation of the acrylate π-system to the incoming diene. The key advancement over conventional directed evolution is not simply increased rigidity; it is conditional, geometry-validated conformational narrowing that selectively stabilizes one diastereomeric transition-state (TS) geometry. We will a priori nominate anchor pairs using pre-registered structural metrics (distance/approach vector distributions, effective molarity proxies, and computed NAC frequency) and validate that the engineered electrostatic asymmetry (field programming) measurably differentiates competing TS geometries via QM/MM or EVB-level modeling across an acrylate panel. Finally, we will explicitly benchmark whether the solution-state stapled NAC restriction reproduces selectivity gains typically associated with lattice-imposed restriction (trans-crystallization/solid-state constraints), without adopting solid-phase catalysis as the primary method.
Plan:
Step 0 — Define reaction system, readouts, and a priori decision criteria
0.1 Model reaction: cyclopentadiene (or 1,3-cyclohexadiene as a slower comparator) + an acrylate panel designed to separate electronic vs steric contributions to enantiodifferentiation. Panel (minimum): methyl acrylate, tert-butyl acrylate, benzyl acrylate; α-methyl acrylate; β-methyl acrylate; and at least 4 para-substituted aryl acrylates spanning Hammett σp (e.g., p-OMe, p-Me, H, p-F, p-CF3) where solubility allows.
0.2 Primary performance metrics (pre-registered):
- Enantioselectivity: ee and E-value (or enantiomeric ratio er converted to E when appropriate).
- Catalysis: kcat, KM, kcat/KM under steady-state; single-turnover rate where feasible.
- Stapling behavior: crosslink fraction fXL (LC–MS intact mass) as a function of time and substrate presence.
- Conformational narrowing: Δσdistance from DEER/smFRET (distance distribution width) and HDX protection factor changes.
0.3 Go/no-go criteria for “binding-gated” success:
- Gating specificity: fXL(bound) / fXL(apo) ≥ 10 within 30 min at screening conditions (or, for reversible staples, Kd,app difference: KXL(bound) / KXL(apo) ≥ 10).
- Functional coupling: variants must show a positive monotonic relationship between ee and fXL (time-resolved or condition-resolved) with R ≥ 0.7 across at least 5 timepoints/conditions.
- Not generic rigidification: a constitutively stapled control (anchors forced close) must not fully recapitulate the ee gain unless it also reproduces the same NAC/pose constraints computationally and experimentally.

Step 1 — Scaffold selection and ensemble generation with quantitative geometric constraints
1.1 Select a Diels–Alderase scaffold (natural or designed) with detectable baseline turnover on a benchmark acrylate (≥0.01–0.1 min−1 apparent turnover in crude lysate is acceptable for screening). If no known scaffold meets this, start from a published de novo DA enzyme family and validate activity on the benchmark pair.
1.2 Build multi-state conformational ensembles:
- Apo ensemble: AF2 + molecular dynamics (MD) (e.g., 3–5 replicas, 200–500 ns each) to quantify baseline gate motion.
- Bound ensemble: restrained docking or metadynamics to near-attack conformations (NACs) for each acrylate class; generate ≥200 bound poses per substrate.
1.3 Pre-register geometric anchor constraints for staple placement (screened in silico before wet-lab):
- Apo/open state distance between reactive atoms: d_open ≥ 10–14 Å (to suppress off-state stapling).
- Bound/closed productive NAC state distance: d_closed in the chemistry-specific reactive window (see Step 2): typically 3.0–6.5 Å depending on linkage.
- Approach vector constraint: reactive atoms must achieve an attack angle window consistent with the staple chemistry (e.g., for thiol–Michael/thiol–disulfide exchange type reactions, enforce near-collinearity constraints; for boronate ester formation, enforce B–O coordination geometry).
- Specificity of closure: in the bound ensemble, ≥70% of productive NAC poses place anchors in the reactive window, while ≤10% of nonproductive/off-pathway poses do.
1.4 Compute NAC frequency and pose entropy metrics (pre-registered):
- NAC definition: distance between diene termini and acrylate C=C within 3.2–3.8 Å, and reactive alignment angle within ±20° of the preferred approach for endo pathway.
- Calculate P(NAC) for each substrate and each designed variant; target ≥5× increase in P(NAC) vs unstapled parent as nomination threshold.

Step 2 — Staple chemistry: explicitly reversible vs irreversible strategies aligned to turnover
2.1 Reversible (steady-state gated) staple options (primary path; choose one based on compatibility with scaffold and expression):
Option R1 — Reversible disulfide exchange “dynamic staple” in a shielded pocket:
- Engineer two cysteines at anchors positioned such that disulfide formation is feasible only in the closed, substrate-bound state (d_closed ~ 4.0–6.5 Å S–S with correct dihedral feasibility; d_open ≥ 12 Å).
- Run catalysis under a defined redox buffer that permits exchange (e.g., GSH/GSSG or low mM β-mercaptoethanol tuned to allow disulfide reshuffling). Decision criterion: the disulfide must re-equilibrate on a timescale comparable to or faster than catalytic turnover (t1/2,XL ≤ 1–5× tcat).
Option R2 — Reversible boronate ester tether via genetically encoded p-boronophenylalanine (pBpa analogs) + cis-diol UAA partner:
- Install a boronic-acid-bearing UAA at anchor-1 and a cis-diol-bearing UAA at anchor-2; boronate ester formation is reversible and sensitive to microenvironment/pH. Target bound-state effective molarity high enough for >50% tethering in the closed state, but minimal in apo.
- Decision criterion: demonstrate pH-dependent and competitive-diol “destapling” without global denaturation.
2.2 Irreversible (maturation/locking) staple options (secondary path; explicitly treated as priming-to-mature catalyst):
Option I1 — Fast intramolecular IEDDA (tetrazine–strained alkene) UAA pair:
- Select anchors where d_closed supports rapid intramolecular reaction (effective molarity proxy from MD; require that the reactive atoms reside within 3.0–5.0 Å for ≥50% of productive NAC frames).
- Operational plan: produce enzyme in unstapled form, prime with acrylate to induce closure and drive stapling, then remove excess substrate and characterize the “matured” catalyst.
Option I2 — Proximity-enabled thioether formation (electrophilic UAA + Cys):
- Use an electrophilic UAA (anchor-1) with tuned reactivity to minimize off-state reaction; require d_open ≥ 14 Å and solvent shielding in closed state.
- Same priming/maturation evaluation as I1.
2.3 Explicit turnover-coupling tests for each chemistry (pre-registered):
- For reversible staples: measure fXL at steady state during catalysis; require cyclical behavior (fXL changes with substrate presence and relaxes after substrate removal).
- For irreversible staples: quantify catalytic parameters before priming, during priming, and after complete stapling; treat post-stapled enzyme as the functional state and directly compare to constitutively stapled geometrically forced controls.

Step 3 — Anchor nomination and library architecture with quantitative filters
3.1 Use HotSpot Wizard 3.0-style hotspot selection on the chosen scaffold, but add staple-specific geometric scoring:
- Filter mutations by ΔΔG (FoldX/Rosetta): include only anchors and nearby substitutions with predicted ΔΔG ≤ +1.5 kcal/mol unless compensated by stabilizing mutations.
- Anchor pair score = w1·P(d_closed in window) − w2·P(d_open in window) + w3·P(NAC) − w4·P(off-pathway closure).
3.2 Focused library modules (built sequentially to preserve interpretability):
Module A (anchor geometry): 2 anchor positions ± 1 adjacent position each to tune closure; include linker-length variants if using UAA pairs.
Module B (electrostatic field): 3–6 positions chosen by computed electrostatic potential differences between competing TS geometries (see Step 4).
Module C (approach corridor): 3–6 positions shaping endo/exo and Re/Si access; conservative hydrophobic/steric substitutions.
3.3 Screening triage: first screen for gating specificity (fXL(bound)/fXL(apo)), then for conversion, then for ee, maintaining a requirement that ee improvement tracks gating.

Step 4 — Explicit TS/electrostatics modeling to justify enantiodifferentiation mechanism
4.1 Construct diastereomeric TS models for the DA reaction in the enzyme active site (endo pathways at minimum; exo as control) for representative acrylates (at least one small alkyl acrylate and one aryl acrylate).
4.2 Compute enantiodifferentiation predictions:
- Use QM/MM (DFT region including diene+dieneophile and key polar residues) or EVB-calibrated barriers.
- Output metrics (pre-registered): ΔΔG‡(Re vs Si) and its sensitivity to staple state (stapled vs unstapled conformations), plus electrostatic potential at key atoms (carbonyl O, alkene carbons) and dispersion/shape complementarity descriptors.
- Nomination criterion: designs advanced to wet-lab must show predicted ΔΔG‡ ≥ 1.0 kcal/mol favoring the target enantiomer in stapled state and ≤0.3 kcal/mol in unstapled state (i.e., selectivity emerges from the stapled conformer).
4.3 Electrostatic “triad” becomes a computationally specified motif:
- Identify one H-bond donor/oxyanion-hole contributor with stable geometry only in the closed+stapled state (occupancy ≥70% in MD), plus one cationic or dipolar residue positioned to bias one TS face; quantify via electric-field projection along the forming bond axis (field-on-bond analysis).

Step 5 — Experiments that directly distinguish conformational narrowing from generic rigidification
5.1 Time-resolved coupling of ee to stapling extent:
- For each top candidate, run reactions while sampling at multiple times; measure fXL (LC–MS) and ee (chiral LC/GC) at each timepoint. Requirement: ee increases with fXL in the same sample series.
5.2 Single-turnover vs steady-state:
- Compare ee and rate under single-turnover (enzyme excess) vs steady-state. If stapling merely “matures” the enzyme, the major ee change should appear after priming rather than differing between regimes; if truly reversible gated, ee should track substrate presence and steady-state cycling.
5.3 Reversible destapling control (mandatory):
- For disulfide-based reversible staple: shift redox to favor reduction after establishing activity; verify loss of fXL and concomitant reversion of ee toward the unstapled baseline without major loss of folded structure.
- For boronate ester: add competitive diol or shift pH to disrupt tether; again require correlated ee change.
5.4 Constitutively stapled/rigidified controls:
- Engineer a forced-close variant (e.g., short peptide insertion or disulfide in a location that closes regardless of substrate) matched for overall rigidity; if it increases stability but not ee (or lacks NAC enrichment), this supports narrowing/pose control as the driver.

Step 6 — Benchmarking against trans-crystallization / solid-state constraint surrogate
6.1 Implement a “lattice-like constraint” surrogate without adopting full trans-crystallization as the main method:
- Immobilize enzyme variants on a support (e.g., mild covalent immobilization or high-affinity binding tag capture) to restrict large-scale motion; or perform microcrystalline enzyme assays if feasible.
6.2 Compare ee and P(NAC)-linked metrics across: (i) free solution unstapled, (ii) free solution stapled, (iii) immobilized/constraint surrogate unstapled, (iv) immobilized/constraint surrogate stapled.
- Success criterion: solution stapling reproduces (or exceeds) any ee gain seen in the constraint surrogate, supporting the claim that stapling mimics beneficial conformational restriction otherwise achieved in crystalline/solid-state settings.

Step 7 — Kinetic decomposition across substrate panel and process-relevant robustness
7.1 Measure kcat, KM, kcat/KM and enantioselective rate ratios across the acrylate panel for:
- Unstapled control (nonreactive anchors), reversible stapled design, irreversible matured design (post-priming), and constitutive rigidification control.
7.2 Inhibition/product binding:
- Determine Ki for product and substrate inhibition; test whether stapling reduces off-pathway binding by reducing pose multiplicity (correlate Ki changes with HDX/DEER narrowing).
7.3 Non-conventional media tolerance:
- Test low % organic cosolvents/biphasic conditions; document whether stapling improves operational stability without sacrificing ee (separating stability benefit from selectivity mechanism).

Step 8 — Decision gates and iteration
8.1 If reversible staples fail to cycle (no destapling, or t1/2 too slow), formally downselect to maturation/locking hypothesis and optimize priming protocol + post-stapled activity.
8.2 If stapling occurs without substrate (fXL(apo) high), redesign anchors to increase d_open and solvent exposure in apo state, and/or decrease intrinsic reactivity.
8.3 If ee improves without correlation to fXL, prioritize electrostatic/shape redesign guided by QM/MM ΔΔG‡ and NAC metrics; do not claim gating mechanism without meeting correlation criteria.
Feasibility:
1) Turnover-aligned stapling chemistry (addresses reviewer points i–ii): The plan explicitly separates reversible staples (designed to form and break on catalytic timescales, enabling true binding-gated steady-state cycling) from irreversible staples (explicitly reframed as substrate-triggered maturation/locking). For each, we pre-register the kinetic expectations and the corresponding experimental tests (in-catalysis fXL tracking, priming experiments, and destapling). This prevents ambiguity about whether stapling is a one-time event or a catalytic-cycle-coupled switch.

2) Quantitative anchor placement criteria (addresses point iii): Anchor nomination is constrained by explicit apo vs bound distance distributions, approach vector constraints, and off-pathway closure rejection. We define target Å windows for d_open and d_closed and require that productive NAC poses—but not nonproductive ones—bring anchors into the reactive geometry. These quantitative constraints are enforced before library construction and are later validated by DEER/smFRET/HDX-MS.

3) Direct causal tests for conformational narrowing vs rigidification (addresses point iii & mandatory item 3): The design includes time-resolved ee vs fXL coupling in the same samples, single-turnover vs steady-state comparisons to distinguish priming/maturation from cycling gating, and a mandatory reversible destapling control that should revert ee if narrowing is the driver. Constitutive rigidification controls further separate “stability/rigidity” effects from “pose entropy suppression/NAC enrichment” effects.

4) Explicit TS/electrostatics modeling (addresses point iv & mandatory item 4): The electrostatic-field concept is upgraded into an explicit computational work package: QM/MM or EVB calculations on diastereomeric TS geometries in stapled vs unstapled conformations, with pre-registered advancement thresholds (predicted ΔΔG‡ enantiodifferentiation and field-on-bond/occupancy metrics). This directly tests whether electrostatic asymmetry contributes meaningfully for acrylate DA versus purely steric/dispersion effects, and it guides which residues belong in the “field” module.

5) Trans-crystallization link integrated empirically (addresses mandatory item 5): Rather than rhetorically rejecting trans-crystallization, we benchmark against a solid-state/constraint surrogate (immobilization or microcrystalline assay) to test the central mechanistic claim: that selectivity gains come from conformational restriction/NAC enrichment. Demonstrating that solution stapling reproduces lattice-like selectivity gains strengthens the proposal’s evidentiary chain while keeping the primary method solution-based.

6) Practicality and risk control: The proposal is structured with decision gates (reversible vs maturation mode downselection; off-target stapling redesign; ee–fXL causality requirement) to reduce the probability of spending effort on non-informative variants. The use of HotSpot Wizard-style hotspotting with ΔΔG filters and focused libraries keeps experimental scope tractable while maintaining mechanistic interpretability. The approach remains aligned with established biocatalysis principles for substrate specificity and stereocontrol (Assets 1–2) while explicitly addressing operational robustness and non-conventional media considerations (Asset 3).
Critique: The proposal is unusually well-specified in its mechanistic claims and in the falsifiable coupling tests (ee vs fXL correlation, destapling reversibility, constitutive rigidification controls). The strongest element is the operational separation of reversible gating vs irreversible maturation and the insistence on time-resolved, within-sample causality—this directly addresses the common failure mode where crosslinking merely stabilizes an inactive/altered conformer. However, feasibility risk remains high in two places: (i) achieving truly catalytic-timescale reversible covalent chemistry in a buried protein pocket under turnover conditions (disulfide exchange kinetics/redox control and boronate ester kinetics/pH sensitivity may not match DA turnover), and (ii) assuming that conformational narrowing alone can deliver large ΔΔG‡ enantiodifferentiation for acrylate DA without a more concrete, scaffold-validated catalytic motif for rate acceleration (baseline activity requirement is modest but still a major gating uncertainty). The ‘trans-crystallization’ linkage is handled indirectly; immobilization/microcrystal assays are a reasonable surrogate but do not fully ground claims about lattice-imposed NAC selection unless you demonstrate an actual crystalline enzyme state with measured ee shifts or at least show that the surrogate produces the same conformational signatures as stapling (e.g., identical DEER/HDX patterns). Computationally, QM/MM/EVB is appropriate, but the plan does not specify calibration/validation against experimental barriers or against known DAases, leaving risk that predicted ΔΔG‡ thresholds are not reliable enough to triage libraries.

Hypothesis:
In mitochondrial-disorder hPSCs, an altered αKG-dependent dioxygenase environment during hepatic specification (low effective nuclear αKG, elevated succinate/2-HG competition, and ROS-linked depletion of labile Fe2+) slows the *kinetic turnover* of H3K27me3 at hepatic lineage enhancers/promoters, particularly at the HNF1A regulatory landscape, thereby sustaining PRC2/Polycomb repression long enough to miss the developmental “opening” window in which FOXA2/HNF4A pioneer activity normally stabilizes a hepatoblast-to-hepatocyte trajectory. This yields low-fidelity hepatocyte programs with impaired nitrogen/aromatic amino-acid handling and metabolite buffering, which can secondarily exacerbate neuronal oxidative stress and metabolic instability.

To overcome the reviewers’ feasibility concerns, we replace the abstract succinate/αKG + redox logic gate with a build-testable, quantitatively benchmarked, dual-control system that converts mitochondrial/metabolic state into a *closed-loop, stage-restricted JMJD3 catalytic permission signal* using only validated molecular parts:

(1) A validated NADH/NAD+ proxy biosensor (nuclear-targeted SoNar) provides a quantitative readout of “ETC-reduced” vs “ETC-permissive” states that correlates with mitochondrial dysfunction and differentiation-stage metabolic transitions. SoNar’s ratiometric signal is used to drive an external, calibrated actuator (optogenetic or chemical inducer) rather than relying on an unvalidated metabolite-binding NLS switch.

(2) A validated redox-responsive nuclear export control (Keap1–Nrf2 ETGE/DLG degron logic or an H2O2-responsive OxyR-based switch) is used only as a *safety interlock* (blocks activation under high nuclear oxidative stress), explicitly acknowledging that nuclear redox may not be monotonic with mitochondrial ROS and therefore is not used as the primary quantitative gate.

(3) Locus selectivity is not asserted via promiscuous IDRs; instead, catalytic JMJD3 is recruited by a minimal, defined-affinity interaction module to endogenous hepatic TF/cofactor hubs (e.g., MED1- or BRD4-associated enhancer assemblies) using short, characterized binding motifs and direct measurements of nuclear partitioning and JMJD3 occupancy at HNF1A.

Mechanistically, this refined system addresses the key limitation: the mitochondrial disorder creates a transient but decisive mismatch between (i) required JMJD3 demethylation kinetics and (ii) differentiation timing. By enforcing *only-in-window* JMJD3 activity with quantitatively bounded leakiness and direct occupancy verification, we test (a) necessity of αKG/Fe2+-limited JMJD3 kinetics for HNF1A unlocking and (b) sufficiency of temporally localized JMJD3 activity to restore the HNF1A regulon even when metabolic defects persist.
Plan:
Step 0 — Define quantitative success criteria (go/no-go) upfront
0.1 Gate leakiness: in “non-permissive” conditions (mitochondrial-disorder baseline; early DE stage), <5% of cells show reporter-positive JMJD3 activation; protease/actuator off-state cleavage <2% over 24 h.
0.2 Epigenome safety: global H3K27me3 signal change (genome-wide CUT&Tag spike-in normalized) must be ≤10% relative to matched controls; locus-focused effect required: ≥30% reduction at pre-specified hepatic loci (HNF1A, HNF4A targets, PROX1 enhancers) during the permission window.
0.3 Lineage fidelity: off-lineage transcriptional programs (neuronal/mesodermal/intestinal) must remain ≤5% of total UMIs in scRNA-seq at hepatoblast stage; hepatocyte marker module score must increase ≥1 SD over baseline mitochondrial-disorder differentiation.
0.4 Recruitment specificity: JMJD3 occupancy enrichment at HNF1A regulatory elements ≥3-fold over genomic background and ≥2-fold over non-hepatic super-enhancers (CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for JMJD3).

Step 1 — Establish causality of the metabolic→JMJD3→Polycomb→HNF1A chain (epistasis-grade)
1.1 Cell panels and differentiation: mitochondrial-disorder iPSCs spanning nuclear-encoded ETC (Complex I/IV) and mtDNA variants; isogenic corrected controls where feasible; healthy donors. Use identical passage windows and synchronized hepatic differentiation (DE → hepatic specification → hepatoblast → HLC). Sample every 24 h days 0–10, with denser sampling (every 12 h) during hepatic specification (e.g., days 3–6 depending on protocol).

1.2 Quantify the putative dioxygenase constraint with direct nuclear relevance:
  - Targeted metabolomics (LC–MS): αKG, succinate, fumarate, 2-HG in whole-cell and nuclear-enriched fractions (validate fraction purity by Lamin A/C enrichment).
  - Labile Fe2+: nuclear and cytosolic labile Fe2+ using FerroOrange (plus orthogonal ICP-MS for total iron if needed).
  - Redox: nuclear H2O2 with nuclear HyPer7; mitochondrial superoxide with MitoSOX; NADH/NAD+ proxy with SoNar targeted to nucleus and cytosol.
  - Bioenergetics: Seahorse OCR/ECAR; lactate release.

1.3 Measure endogenous JMJD3 behavior directly (not only histone marks):

Feasibility:
Addresses critique (1): We remove the unvalidated succinate/αKG NLS sensor. Instead, we use a validated, ratiometric NADH/NAD+ proxy biosensor (SoNar) to *measure* metabolic state and couple it to a calibrated, externally controllable protease actuator (optogenetic or chemical). This is build-testable immediately, with explicit dynamic-range, response-time, and leak targets and a direct cleavage reporter.

Addresses critique (2): Nuclear redox is not assumed to monotonically reflect mitochondrial ROS. Redox sensing is demoted to a safety interlock (blocks activation under high nuclear oxidative stress) rather than a primary quantitative gate, reducing confounding by compartment buffering and differentiation-stage redox shifts.

Addresses critique (3): Locus selectivity is no longer predicated on broadly phase-separating IDRs. We adopt minimal, affinity-characterized docking motifs and explicitly compare IDR-free versus minimal-IDR variants, while directly measuring nuclear partitioning and JMJD3 occupancy (CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for JMJD3) at HNF1A and control loci. We set quantitative acceptance criteria for global H3K27me3 change to prevent genome-wide erosion.

Addresses critique (4): Step 1 is upgraded from correlational to epistasis-grade causality: αKG/Fe2+ restoration is tested for rescue *only when JMJD3 is present* (JMJD3 CRISPRi/KO), and enforced JMJD3 activation is tested for rescue *despite persistent metabolic defects* (sufficiency). Parallel measurements of PRC2 (EZH2 occupancy), HDAC state, and pioneer factor binding explicitly evaluate alternative mechanisms.

Addresses critique (5): We add genome-wide and locus-specific engagement assays beyond histone marks: JMJD3 CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN, quantitative cleavage/leak reporters, and pre-registered go/no-go thresholds for global H3K27me3 change, off-lineage transcriptional burden, and activation leakiness.

Grounding in assets: Asset 3 supports that JMJD3 catalytic activity can unlock hepatic programs including HNF1A; our approach constrains this activity temporally and spatially to avoid global demethylation. Assets 1–2 motivate the PSC-based modeling framework and the broader mitochondrial/neurological disease linkage, while our added liver–brain co-culture tests provide a mechanistic bridge from hepatic rescue to neuronal stress phenotypes relevant in mitochondrial disorders.
Critique: The engineering plan is unusually concrete (quantified leak targets, spike-in normalized CUT&Tag thresholds, cleavage reporter kinetics, safe-harbor integration, and explicit control constructs) and directly addresses prior feasibility critiques. However, several high-risk assumptions remain insufficiently deconvolved: (i) SoNar (NADH/NAD+) is an indirect proxy for the relevant nuclear αKG/succinate/2-HG/Fe2+ dioxygenase constraints; closed-loop actuation based on SoNar may misclassify the true JMJD3-permissive window across genotypes and stages, undermining the central ‘permission’ concept. (ii) The proposed locus-selective recruitment via short MED1/BRD4-associated motifs is under-specified and plausibly non-selective at the genome scale (MED1/BRD4 hubs are widespread); without a pre-registered panel of off-target loci and quantitative occupancy selectivity metrics beyond “2-fold over non-hepatic super-enhancers,” the risk of broad chromatin perturbation remains. (iii) The autoinhibitory ‘cage’ for the JMJD3 catalytic domain is described at a schematic level; steric blocking that is tight enough to meet <2%/24h leak yet fully reversible with fast TEV kinetics is non-trivial and will require extensive protein engineering that is not fully scoped. (iv) The mechanistic claim that slowed H3K27me3 turnover at HNF1A causes a missed pioneer-factor stabilization window is plausible but not uniquely supported; alternative drivers (PRC2 recruitment dynamics, chromatin remodelers, DNA methylation, or impaired FOXA2/HNF4A expression/activation) could generate the same phenotype, and the current ‘rule-out’ set does not yet include the strongest competing causal nodes (e.g., DNMT/TET balance, SWI/SNF/BAF occupancy, enhancer RNA output). Overall, the proposal is strong and testable, but its core control variable (SoNar-defined permissivity) and its specificity mechanism (BRD4/MED1 docking) remain the primary logical and technical liabilities.

Hypothesis:
A dual-orthogonal, embryo-tunable human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) engineering strategy will increase target-organ human contribution while preventing ectopic human expansion in neonatal interspecies chimeras generated by blastocyst complementation by (i) implementing an *orthogonal small-molecule-inducible metabolic–epigenetic compatibility governor* that buffers peri-implantation hypoxia/2-OG-dioxygenase stress (including DMOG-like background PHD inhibition) without using DMOG as the control input, and (ii) deploying a *hardened, multi-layer containment architecture* combining a constitutive failsafe suicide switch plus a small set of empirically validated, cross-species-conserved lineage-restricted thymidine kinase (TK) ablation elements with quantified leakiness and developmental timing.

Mechanistic rationale addressing prior fragilities:
1) **Input orthogonality and clampability**: Rather than sensing DMOG (which is intrinsically confounded by oxygen, αKG/succinate ratio, Fe2+/ascorbate, and embryo microenvironment), the governor is actuated by a ligand–receptor pair that is orthogonal to mammalian metabolism (e.g., rapalog-induced dimerization or trimethoprim-stabilized DD). DMOG is treated only as a *background perturbation* that the circuit buffers. This decouples the *control input* from embryo variable physiology and makes a bounded “compatibility state” achievable with a defined transfer function.
2) **Biologically implementable circuit dynamics**: The governor is engineered as a *two-loop controller* (fast induction + delayed negative feedback) with explicitly parameterized response time, amplitude, and noise, such that protective modules turn on within the embryo peri-implantation window while preventing sustained HIF-like maladaptive transcriptional states.
3) **Containment robustness**: Instead of complex multi-input CRISPR logic with high in vivo leakage risk, containment is simplified to (a) an always-available orthogonal failsafe suicide switch for catastrophic shutdown, and (b) a minimal number of lineage promoter/enhancer modules chosen for cross-species conservation and empirically characterized ROC/leak curves in pig embryos/ex vivo gastrulation models. Prohibited lineages are targeted at the earliest transcriptionally detectable stage *before colonization becomes effectively irreversible*, and early migratory escape is addressed by adding an early-window “germline/ectoderm sentinel” ablation layer.
4) **In vivo pharmacology and escape management**: Ganciclovir (GCV) timing, dosing, placental transfer, and on/off kinetics are explicitly mapped with PK sampling and linked to reporter-based real-time TK expression readouts; cassette silencing/escape is monitored by longitudinal ddPCR for integrity, single-cell reporter quantification, and enrichment checks for resistant clones.

Collectively, these modifications preserve the original concept chain—metabolic/epigenetic buffering to improve peri-implantation fitness plus post hoc ablation to prevent ectopic contribution—while removing the DMOG-sensor confound, quantifying circuit dynamics, hardening containment logic, and concretizing fetal drug exposure and escape surveillance.

Step 0 — Model choice, ethical boundary conditions, and baseline chimera performance mapping
0.1 Choose a stringent blastocyst complementation niche with established developmental constraint and measurable organ function endpoints:
  - Primary: porcine PDX1-/- (pancreas) or SALL1-/- (kidney).
  - Define prohibited tissues a priori: CNS (forebrain/midbrain/hindbrain), germline (gonadal ridge, PGC markers), and any ectopic epithelial/mesenchymal expansions.
0.2 Establish baseline with non-engineered primed hPSCs vs “chimera-competent” benchmark (e.g., naïve-like hPSC state if permitted) to quantify:
  - Early retention/apoptosis (24–120 h post-injection), spatial localization, and proliferation.
  - Mid-gestation tissue distribution (ddPCR human DNA; immunostaining; pilot scRNA-seq) to determine the earliest timepoint where prohibited lineages become transcriptionally detectable.

Step 1 — Build orthogonal compatibility governor (DMOG = disturbance, not input)
1.1 Genomic architecture (two safe-harbor sites; single copy; insulated):
  - Site A (e.g., AAVS1): Orthogonal actuator + governor program.
  - Site B (e.g., CLYBL): Containment modules + reporters.
  - Use strong insulators (e.g., cHS4 or equivalent) flanking each cassette; verify single-copy insertion by long-read sequencing spanning junctions.

1.2 Actuation modality (choose one and lock it early; both are orthogonal):
  Option 1: **Rapalog-inducible dimerization** (FRB/FKBP) controlling a synthetic transcription factor (synTF).
    - Architecture: synTF = DNA-binding domain (e.g., dCas9 to fixed gRNAs or a synthetic zinc-finger array) split into two halves fused to FRB and FKBP; rapalog drives assembly.
    - Advantage: rapid ON kinetics (minutes), tunable by ligand concentration, reversible.
  Option 2: **Trimethoprim (TMP)-stabilized degron (DHFR-DD)** controlling synTF abundance.
    - Architecture: synTF fused to DHFR-DD; TMP stabilizes; withdrawal yields rapid degradation.
    - Advantage: direct abundance control; simple dose-response.

1.3 Governor program (explicitly bounded “compatibility state”):
  - Outputs are modular and limited to a small, testable set with direct mechanistic ties to peri-implantation attrition:
    (i) Redox/anoikis protection: e.g., controlled expression of catalase/SOD2 or NRF2-axis activator (bounded).
    (ii) Mitochondrial support/anaplerosis: controlled expression of a mild anaplerotic enhancer (e.g., pyruvate carboxylase upshift) avoiding broad metabolic rewiring.
    (iii) Epigenetic flux buffering: increase availability of αKG equivalents via mild transporter/enzymatic tuning (bounded), with explicit monitoring of αKG/succinate ratio.
  - Add a *HIF-output limiter* without attempting to “sense DMOG”: implement repression of a small panel of maladaptive glycolytic/HIF targets (pre-identified in baseline embryos) via synTF-driven CRISPRi.

1.4 Dynamics shaping (quantitative, parameterized):
  - Implement a **two-loop controller**:
    Fast loop: ligand → synTF ON (tON target: 15–60 min in vitro; 1–2 h in embryo culture).
    Slow loop: synTF induces delayed negative feedback (e.g., inducible expression of a repressor or an shRNA targeting synTF mRNA) with delay τ set by using an intron-containing transcript and a weak promoter.
  - Design targets (to be achieved and verified):
    - Peak-to-baseline fold-change of key outputs: 2–5× (avoid supra-physiologic expression).
    - Pulse width: 6–18 h after a single ligand exposure; reversible to baseline within 24–36 h after withdrawal.
    - Cell-to-cell variability: CV < 0.35 for synTF reporter at peak (measured by flow cytometry).

Step 2 — Quantify transfer function, noise, and predictive minimal model (in vitro then ex vivo embryo)
2.1 In vitro disturbance-testing panel (DMOG as stressor; also hypoxia and succinate):
  - Conditions: normoxia vs 1–5% O2; ± DMOG (dose range chosen to mimic embryo-exposure stress), ± succinate elevation, low nutrient, dissociation/shear stress.
  - Readouts (time-resolved, single-cell where possible):
    - Metabolomics: αKG, succinate, 2-HG; compute αKG/succinate ratio.
    - Dioxygenase-linked epigenetics: global and locus-specific histone marks (e.g., H3K27me3/H3K4me3 panels) + DNA methylation proxies.
    - HIF program: targeted transcript panel and reporter.
    - Survival: caspase activation, anoikis assays, mitochondrial membrane potential.

2.2 System identification (explicit modeling requirement):
  - Fit a minimal ODE or state-space model linking ligand input → synTF abundance/activity → output modules → survival proxy under disturbances.
  - Extract: EC50 for ligand, Hill coefficient, t1/2 ON/OFF, hysteresis, and noise propagation (report as transfer curves and distributions).
  - Use the model to choose an embryo-compatible ligand dosing schedule that achieves a bounded protective pulse without sustained reprogramming.

2.3 Ex vivo embryo culture validation (predictive control):
  - Inject engineered hPSCs into host blastocysts; apply ligand pulse schedule predicted from 2.2 (not DMOG).
  - Add DMOG only as a controlled disturbance arm to show buffering.
  - Validate that measured embryo-level outputs match model predictions within pre-specified tolerance (e.g., ±20% on synTF reporter AUC; ±25% on apoptosis reduction).

Step 3 — Hardened containment: dual-layer safety + simplified lineage restriction with empirical ROC curves
3.1 Layer 1 (constitutive failsafe; orthogonal drug):
  - Introduce an independent suicide switch activated by a second drug distinct from GCV (e.g., inducible caspase-9 with AP1903/rimiducid), driven by a constitutive promoter active in all hPSC derivatives.
  - Purpose: absolute shutdown if unexpected widespread human contribution occurs.

3.2 Layer 2 (GCV/TK-based lineage containment; simplified and empirically validated):
  - Replace complex multi-input CRISPR logic with **a small panel of promoters/enhancers** selected for:
    (i) cross-species conservation of regulatory logic,
    (ii) early activation in prohibited lineages,
    (iii) low/quantifiable leak in target organ progenitors.
  - Proposed minimal set (to be empirically down-selected):
    - Prohibited ectoderm/CNS sentinel: early neural markers (e.g., SOX1/PAX6 enhancer elements validated in pig embryo context).
    - Prohibited germline sentinel: PGC-associated regulatory elements (e.g., PRDM14/DPPA3-associated enhancer logic—final choice contingent on pig embryo expression conservation).
    - Optional mesendoderm off-target sentinel if baseline shows diversion.
  - Each sentinel drives TK plus a bright reporter (e.g., nuclear fluorescent protein) via 2A, enabling direct leak quantification.

3.3 ROC/leak characterization before in vivo use:
  - In vitro differentiation series into target organ progenitors vs prohibited lineages; compute:
    - Sensitivity: fraction of prohibited-lineage cells that activate sentinel.
    - Specificity: fraction of on-target progenitors that remain sentinel-negative.
    - Determine thresholding strategy (e.g., minimal promoter variants, enhancer truncations) to achieve pre-specified operating point (e.g., >95% sensitivity at <1% leak into on-target progenitors).

3.4 Developmental timing map (detectability vs irreversibility):
  - Using baseline chimera and ex vivo embryo data, map:
    - t_detect: first time prohibited lineage transcripts/reporters become reliably detectable in human donor cells.
    - t_commit: earliest time when prohibited colonization becomes spatially established (migration/settlement markers).
  - Select GCV window(s) such that t_treat ≤ t_commit and after initial niche occupancy for on-target lineage.

Step 4 — In vivo blastocyst complementation with defined ligand and GCV regimens
4.1 Embryo procedure:
  - Inject equal numbers of engineered vs control hPSCs into niche-deficient blastocysts.
  - Apply orthogonal ligand pulse (rapalog or TMP) during pre-transfer embryo culture to induce compatibility governor; washout prior to transfer.
  - Include DMOG-disturbance arm (optional) to demonstrate buffering rather than control.

4.2 GCV pharmacokinetic (PK) and delivery plan (explicit):
  - Route comparison pilot: maternal systemic (IV/SC) vs direct fetal/neonatal (if ethically/technically allowed).
  - Quantify placental transfer and fetal exposure:
    - Serial sampling: maternal plasma, amniotic fluid (where feasible), fetal plasma/tissue at defined timepoints.
    - LC–MS/MS quantification of GCV.
  - Define dosing by target fetal exposure above TK EC50 window while below toxicity thresholds (guided by sentinel reporter dynamics and fetal safety endpoints).

4.3 Anti-escape/silencing monitoring:
  - Link TK to reporter (2A) for direct expression tracking.
  - Longitudinal ddPCR:
    - Cassette copy number/integrity in recovered tissues.
    - Quantify enrichment of cassette-negative human cells post-GCV (escape signal).
  - scRNA-seq in selected timepoints to detect transcriptional silencing signatures and lineage escape.

5.1 Efficacy endpoints:
  - Early embryo: retention, apoptosis, localization, donor cell cycling fraction.
  - Mid-gestation/neonatal: organ-specific human contribution (ddPCR; species-resolved scRNA-seq; IHC).

  - Whole-body mapping of human cells with emphasis on CNS and gonads.
  - Teratoma/lesion surveillance.

  - Failsafe validation: ability to ablate all human cells via iCasp9 if triggered.

  - Mixed-effects models (litter/surrogate as random effects).

  - Gate A: Governor transfer function meets targets (tON, pulse width, CV, bounded output) and improves survival under disturbance in vitro.

1) Addressing the DMOG-sensor confound (reviewer point i): The revised governor does not attempt DMOG specificity. Instead, it uses a truly orthogonal inducer (rapalog or TMP) with well-defined pharmacology and receptor specificity in mammalian systems. DMOG is repositioned strictly as a disturbance to be buffered, aligning the design with the reality that DMOG broadly inhibits 2-OG dioxygenases and is heavily confounded by embryo microenvironment variables.

2) Implementable kinetics and low-noise operation (reviewer point ii): The governor is now explicitly parameterized as a two-loop controller with measurable ON/OFF half-times, pulse width, and cell-to-cell variability targets. The plan includes system identification (transfer function extraction) and a minimal predictive model validated first in vitro and then in ex vivo embryo culture. This directly de-risks claims of amplitude clamping by converting them into quantified, testable design specifications.

3) Containment logic de-risking (reviewer point iii & v): The containment strategy is simplified away from fragile multiplex CRISPR logic toward (a) a constitutive orthogonal failsafe (e.g., iCasp9) and (b) a small set of empirically validated lineage sentinels whose leakiness is quantified via ROC curves in both target and prohibited differentiation contexts. The proposal explicitly maps when prohibited lineages become detectable versus when colonization becomes hard to reverse, and schedules GCV pulses accordingly to address early migratory escape.

4) Concrete GCV pharmacology and fetal safety (reviewer point iv): The revised plan includes a PK program (route comparison, LC–MS/MS quantification, placental transfer assessment) and ties dosing schedules to reporter-verified TK activation and developmental timing. Pulsed dosing is chosen to reduce continuous selective pressure that would otherwise favor TK silencing/escape.

5) Escape/silencing surveillance: Reporter-linked TK expression, ddPCR cassette integrity, and scRNA-seq-based detection of silencing states provide multiple orthogonal readouts to detect and quantify escape. The inclusion of a constitutive failsafe provides a backstop even if TK modules partially fail.

6) Alignment to empirical foundations (assets): The buffering objective is grounded in evidence that αKG-dependent dioxygenases link metabolism to chromatin state and differentiation kinetics in primed hPSCs and that succinate/DMOG-like dioxygenase inhibition can derail differentiation/epigenetic homeostasis (Asset 1). The chimera/blastocyst complementation setting and its key bottlenecks (peri-implantation attrition; low contribution) are aligned with the interspecies chimera literature (Assets 2–3). The suicide-gene approach is grounded in validated TK/prodrug ablation in PSC contexts and emphasizes selective ablation design and pharmacologic considerations (Asset 4), now extended with a separate orthogonal failsafe to satisfy reviewer safety expectations.
Critique:
The proposal is technically ambitious and substantially improves on common fragilities in chimera-control concepts by introducing (i) true input orthogonality and (ii) explicit dynamical specifications plus system identification. However, key scientific risks remain under-specified at the level needed for high confidence: (1) The choice of governor outputs (redox/anoikis protection, anaplerosis, αKG buffering, CRISPRi of HIF targets) is plausible but not yet tied to a minimal, causal set of embryo-validated failure modes with clearly ranked contributions; without a prioritized causal graph, the controller may stabilize survival at the cost of altered lineage bias or increased competitive fitness outside the target niche. (2) The two-loop controller is described conceptually but lacks concrete molecular implementations with expected parameter ranges (e.g., promoter strengths, degron half-lives in hPSC derivatives, feedback gain limits) and does not address developmental-stage–dependent silencing of safe-harbor transgenes in vivo, which can break both governor and containment. (3) Cross-species conservation of proposed sentinel regulatory elements (SOX1/PAX6, PRDM14/DPPA3 logic) is a major unresolved dependency; enhancer logic frequently diverges across species and developmental context, and ROC curves in vitro may not predict in vivo activation timing in pig embryos (risk: late activation after migration/settlement). (4) The GCV/TK containment plan is strengthened by PK mapping, but the feasibility of achieving a fetal exposure window that is simultaneously effective, non-toxic, and temporally precise—especially across variable gestational pharmacokinetics—remains uncertain; selection for TK silencing/escape may still be substantial, and the stated <5% cassette-loss enrichment threshold lacks justification relative to acceptable residual prohibited contribution.
